summaries.example: Imagine two identical plates of food placed the same distance from a hungry donkey. If the donkey has no reason to prefer one, how could it choose? This story is linked to Buridan, although the exact story is not found in his own writings. It was probably created later to make fun of his ideas about choice.
summaries.summary: John Buridan was an important philosopher and university teacher in Paris during the 1300s. He taught logic and explained the works of Aristotle, but he also wrote his own studies. His best-known work was a very large guide to logic. Buridan believed that language must be studied as people really use it, including jokes, metaphors, confusing sentences, and sentences that talk about themselves. He used this careful study of words to discuss bigger questions about reality and knowledge. In natural philosophy, he developed the theory of impetus to explain why a thrown object keeps moving. In ethics, he studied choice, freedom, the will, and weakness of will. The famous “Buridan’s Ass” story is connected with him, but it was not written by him. His work influenced many later university teachers and thinkers.
key_ideas: John Buridan was a fourteenth-century teacher and philosopher at the University of Paris.
He wrote about language, logic, nature, the mind, and ethics, often using careful analysis of sentences.
His large logic book helped spread a newer style of medieval logic across Europe.
He explained a thrown object’s motion by saying it receives an inner force called impetus.
He thought good choices depend on what the mind understands about the choices.
summaries.why_it_matters: Buridan shows how asking what words mean can improve our thinking about science, decisions, and everyday arguments. His work also reminds us that historical thinkers can be both traditional and inventive: he followed Aristotle in many ways while changing important ideas about motion and logic.

important_terms.definition: A careful way of thinking about arguments and whether conclusions follow from reasons.
A word or phrase standing for something in a particular sentence or situation.
A force or push that helps a moving object keep moving after it is thrown.
A way of thinking that does not add more kinds of things than needed to explain something.

questions_to_think_about: Can a sentence mean different things depending on pauses or context?
When should we add a new explanation, and when should we first check whether we misunderstood the words?
If two choices seem equally good, is waiting a kind of choice?
How can observations help us understand nature?

summaries.example: Consider the argument: “Nothing dead is an animal; some man is dead; therefore, some man is not an animal.” Buridan argues that this may look like a valid syllogism, but the word “man” is being used differently in the premise and conclusion: in the premise it can include past people, while in the conclusion it is read more narrowly. His doctrine of ampliation explains how terms can range over possible, past, or future things in certain contexts.
summaries.summary: John Buridan was a Parisian arts master whose work helped shape later medieval and early modern philosophy. His writings include commentaries on Aristotle, shorter treatises, and the extensive Summulae de dialectica. He reorganized terminist logic around the analysis of propositions, terms, arguments, fallacies, demonstrations, and paradoxical “sophisms.” A central tool was supposition: a term can stand for different things depending on how it is used. Ampliation further explains how expressions may range beyond currently existing objects. This semantic attention to context allowed Buridan to address ambiguity, modal reasoning, and self-reference without assuming that every troublesome phrase names a new entity. His metaphysics is therefore closely tied to his logic and is broadly nominalist, though it also defends real natures and quantitative features when his explanations require them. In natural philosophy, impetus explains projectile motion as the persistence of an impressed internal force, but Buridan did not abandon Aristotelian physics as a whole. In ethics, he examined intellect, will, freedom, weakness of will, and virtue. His account appears to balance intellectualist and voluntarist traditions, yet the intellect remains decisive in determining whether delaying a choice is good. The familiar donkey story is a later association, not a passage from Buridan’s works.
key_ideas: Buridan treated logic as ultimately practical: it teaches methods so that people can use arguments to test conclusions.
He analyzed ordinary spoken and written language instead of replacing it with a perfectly ideal mental language.
His account of supposition and ampliation connected logical validity with context, time, possibility, and the intended meaning of a speaker.
His nominalism rejected independently existing universal things while allowing a substantial role for simple concepts and the natures they express.
His theory of impetus explained projectile motion through an internal force, although he remained committed to important Aristotelian positions.
In ethics, Buridan gave the intellect a central role in choice while describing the will as able to delay action when judgment is uncertain.
summaries.why_it_matters: Buridan’s philosophy illustrates how logic, semantics, metaphysics, natural philosophy, and ethics can support one another. His work is valuable not because it simply predicts modern theories, but because it offers a historically distinct way to analyze inference, language, motion, knowledge, and action. It also cautions against easy labels: Buridan was innovative in particular arguments while remaining deeply connected to Aristotelian methods and medieval university practices.

important_terms.definition: The medieval study of how terms function within propositions, including what they signify and what they stand for in context.
A term’s capacity to stand for or pick out something in a particular proposition or context.
The expansion of what a term can stand for, such as actual, past, future, or possible things, especially in modal contexts.
A philosophical practice that explains claims economically by avoiding unnecessary entities; in Buridan, it is not simply a single doctrine about universals.
A force transmitted to a moving object that helps explain continued motion after the original mover has stopped acting.
A puzzle about a sentence that seems to undermine itself, such as a claim that all propositions are false.
The power to delay a decision when the goodness of the available options is not clear.
A study of being considered through what can be established by human reasoning rather than through revealed articles of faith.

questions_to_think_about: Should a logician analyze language as people actually use it, or reform it into a more precise ideal language?
Why might a change in the temporal range of a term make a syllogism invalid?
Does explaining universals as ways of predicating avoid, or merely relocate, the problem of universals?
Can a theory of free choice give the will independence if the decision to delay must itself be judged good by the intellect?
Why is it misleading to call Buridan simply a forerunner of Galileo?

summaries.example: Suppose someone says, “The word ‘blue’ has four letters.” Here “blue” stands for the word itself, not for a color. But in “The sky is blue,” it stands for a color property. Buridan’s idea of supposition helps explain this difference. He also thought that pauses, context, and a speaker’s intention can change how a sentence should be understood.
summaries.summary: John Buridan was a leading philosopher and teacher in fourteenth-century Paris. He spent his career in the faculty of arts, where he taught logic and Aristotle’s philosophy. Unlike many famous medieval philosophers, he did not produce theological writings. His works include detailed commentaries, critical questions, and the Summulae de dialectica, a large logic textbook that became influential in universities across Europe. Buridan thought logic should help people interpret and test real human speech. Words do not always have one fixed function: a term may refer to an object, to a word, or to a concept, depending on its use. Meaning can also depend on pauses, grammar, surrounding discussion, and a speaker’s intention. This approach helped him handle difficult problems about universals, causation, possibility, and self-reference without automatically inventing extra entities. In natural philosophy, he developed and spread an impetus theory of projectile motion. A thrown object continues moving because it receives an internal force, which weakens through resistance. Buridan remained partly Aristotelian, however, so he should not be described simply as an early modern scientist. In ethics, he examined how intellect and will cooperate in human choice. He emphasized that people may delay action when they are uncertain about which option is better. The later tale of a donkey unable to choose between two equal piles of hay reflects this issue, but the tale does not appear in Buridan’s own writings.
key_ideas: Buridan worked as an arts master at the University of Paris and wrote mainly about philosophy rather than theology.
His major logic work began as a commentary but became an original, wide-ranging textbook used in universities.
He argued that meaning depends on grammar, context, conventional use, and what a speaker intends.
He used logic to challenge the idea that every relation or description must correspond to a separate thing in reality.
His theory of impetus explained continued projectile motion, but he still accepted several major Aristotelian ideas.
His ethics connects freedom with uncertainty: a person can postpone a decision when the good choice is not evident.
summaries.why_it_matters: Buridan matters because he connected close attention to language with large questions about reality, science, and moral action. His work shows that a philosopher can preserve parts of an older tradition while revising other parts. It also teaches us to separate what a thinker actually wrote from stories later people told about that thinker.

important_terms.definition: A system for checking how statements are built and whether an argument supports its conclusion.
What a word or expression brings to the mind or makes understood.
What a term stands for in a particular statement; this can change with the context.
The way a term’s range can expand to include things in the past, future, or merely possible.
A view or method that avoids treating universals as separate things existing outside individual objects.
An impressed force used to explain why a thrown object continues moving.
A puzzle involving a statement that refers to itself or to statements like itself.
The ability to hold back from choosing when the options do not seem clearly better or worse.

questions_to_think_about: Can the same word refer to itself in one sentence and to something else in another?
Why might a careful thinker study ordinary language instead of replacing it with a perfect language?
Does a moving object need an outside mover every moment, or can it carry an internal force?
If someone chooses to wait, what does that tell us about freedom?
Why should we be cautious when a later story becomes attached to a historical philosopher?
